 Enhancement in import duty for protecting domestic industry 
*34l. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have identified any items for enhancing for import 
duty to thwart competition to domestic industry; 
(b) if so, what are the items that have been identified by Government; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (c) Simultaneously with the 
phased removal of import restrictions, Government has been implementing a 
conscious policy of adjustments in customs duties to provide necessary 
protection to the domestic producers. Towards that end, customs duty on almost 
all the items on which QRs were to be re moved was raised to the peak rate of 
35% in the budget for the year 2000-2001. Subsequent to the budget, import 
duty on skimmed milk powder was raised from 0% to 60%, on chicken legs from 
35% to 100%, on rice from 0% to 75%, on arecanut from 35% to 100% and on apple 
from 35% to 50%. Import duty on edible oil was raised twice, in June and again in 
November last year. In the budget for the year 2001 -2002, the customs duty on 
coconut, copra, tea and coffee has been raised from 35% to 70%. The import 
duty on various refined edible oils excepting soyabean oil has been raised to 85%. 
Similarly, the import duty on various crude edible oils excepting soyabean oil has 
been raised to 75%, with a concession of 20% on the imports of crude palm oil 
made by sick Vanaspati Units. The imports are being closely monitored and 
Government will take all appropriate steps including increase in customs duty, 
within the bound rates, whenever the situation so arises.

Import of substandard products 
*342. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state; 
(a) whether Government propose to introduce any scheme to prevent imports 
of substandard quality products in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the measures proposed to be taken by Government to stop dumping of 
cheap goods in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (c) Imports in India, apart from being 
subject to compliance of Export Import Policy; are also subject to compliance of 
the provisions of any other law for the time being in force. Thus, all imported goods 
have to comply with all domestic laws, rules, orders, regulations, technical 
specifications, and environmental safety norms as applicable to domestically 
produced goods. 
In order to prevent import of substandard quality goods into the country, import 
of 131 products has been made subject to compliance of the mandatory Indian quality 
standards as applicable to domestic goods. For compliance of this requirement, all 
manufacturers/exporters of these products to India are required to register themselves 
with the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). The list of 131 products includes various 
food preservatives and additives, milk powder, infant milk food, certain kinds of cement, 
household and similar electrical appliances, gas cylinders and multi-purpose dry 
batteries. 
The imports are being closely monitored and the Government is 
determined to ensure through appropriate use of tariff and other measures that imports 
do not cause any serious injury or detriment to domestic producers. Some of the 
steps taken towards that end are as follows: 
(i)     Custom duties on a nubmer of agricultural and other products have been 
increased; 
(u)     Preliminary antidumping duties have been imposed on import of battery cells 
and sports shoes from China; 
(in)    Import of consumer goods has been made subject to mandatory 
labelling requirements;

(iv)   Counter vailing duty equivalent to the States excise duty is proposed to be 
imposed on import of alcoholic beverages. 
Besides, an Inter-ministerial Groups has been set up under the 
Chairmanship of Commerce Secretary, to examine the likely impact of QR removal on 
domestic producers and to suggest suitable measures to be taken by the

Repeal of SICA 
*343. SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government propose to stop the functioning of 
BIFR and withdraw the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what are the reasons therefor? 
THE  MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALA SAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a)Yes, Sir. 
(b) Based on the recommendations of various committees including Eradi 
Committee on Law Relating to Insolvency and Winding up of Companies and the 
decisions of the Group of Ministers constituted to consider the matter relating to 
repeal of Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, (SICA), the 
Government propose to repeal SICA as per the announcement made in me Budget 
Speech 2001-2002 by Finance Minister. 
(c) The above decision has been taken to remove the lacunae in the existing 
mechanism and to provide the faster mechanism by replacing the Board for Industiral

effective, orderly and expeditious procedure to deal with the matters relating to 
rehabilitation, revival and winding up of the companies and with a view to avoiding 
multiplicity of fora such as Company Law Board, BIFR and High Courts. 
Statutory audit of panchayats and municipalities 
*344. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [20 March, 2001 ] 
(a) Whether Government propose to bring uniformity in all accounting and 
audit arrangements of panchayat and municipalities by bringing them under C AG with 
authority to lay down accounting and auditing standards and general superintendence 
over such audit; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALA SAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) Government have accepted the 
recommendation of the Eleventh Finance Commission that the Comptroller & Auditor 
General of India should be entrusted with the responsibility of exercising control and 
supervision over the proper maintenance of accounts and their audit for all the 
tiers/levels of panchayats and urben local bodies. 
The details of the accepted recomm endation of the Eleventh Finance 
Commission are as under:— 
(i) States should review the existing accounting heads under which funds are 
being transferred to the local bodies. For each such major head/ sub-major 
head, six minor heads should be created-three for the PRIs and another three 
for the ULBs—so that a clear picture of transfers to each category of local 
bodies is readily available. In addition, specific demand heads should be 
created in the State Budgets for the rural and the urban local bodies, 
respectively, wherein transfers to these bodies under various detailed heads 
of account are enlisted. This may be done in consultation with the C & AG 
and the Controller General of Accounts, to ensure uniformity among the 
States. 
(ii)    The C&AG should be entrusted with the responsibility of exercising 
control and supervision over the proper maintenance of accounts and their 
audit for all the tiers/levels of panchayats and urban local bodies. 
(m) The Director, Local Fund Audit or any other agency made responsible for the 
audit of accounts of the local bodies, should work under the technical and 
administrative supervision of the C&AG in the same manner as the Chief 
Electoral Officers of the States operate under the control any supervision of 
the Central Election Commission. In no case should the Director for 
Panchayats or for Urban Local Bodies be entrusted with this work. The 
prescribed authority entrusted with the audit and accounts should not have 
any functional responsibility in

regard to the local bodies, so as to ensure his independence and 
accountability. 
(iv) The C&AG should pr escribe the format for the preparation of budgets

(d) if so, the steps taken to overcome these procedural wrangles? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) to (c) As on 31.12.2000, the 
number of cases pending for adjudication with various departmental 
adjudicating authorities was 27896. Out of these, 14800 cases were pending for

*348. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are formulating an export-friendly 
package of incentives and promotional measures which will be compatible with 
WTO rules; 
(b) whether it will be a medium term strategy to be operational for three to 
five years; and 
(c) if so, what are the details of this policy and whether it will protect the 
industry from international competition especially China? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) The incentives and other 
promotional measures meant for boosting exports in India are export friendly 
and compatible with the WTO frame-wor k. As a result of various measures 
taken in the past to promote exports, the growth rate of exports is 20.7% in 
dollar terms for the period April-Janu ary, 2000-01 as compared to the 
corresponding period of the previous year. The export promotion measures are 
revised every year at the time of announcement of the Exim Policy and necessary 
strategies are formulated to suit the re quirements of the situation. The export 
friendly policies of the Exim policy announced last year include reduction in 
transaction cost through decentralisation, simplification of procedures, setting 
up Special Economic Zones to further boost the exports etc. 
(b) and (c) The medium term export strategy is formulated normally for a 
period of five years which in the present context would be for the period from 
2001-2002 to 2006-2007. This will include examination of the import baskets of 
our major trading partners and commodity and country specificities. Such 
strategic initiatives in the export sector aim at enhancing the competitiveness 
of Indian exports in order to achieve high export growth on a sustained basis.

Changes in Exim Policy 
*351. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
12 

[20March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that some State Governments have urged the Central 
Government to make some changes in the Exim Policy; 
(b) if so, the reasons given for the proposed changes; 
(c) whether Government are ready to accept their suggestions; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCEAND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (d) Some of the State 
Governments have expressed certain reservations regarding removal of QRs on 
714 items which may affect the economy of the respective States. The States 
which have expressed these reservations include Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, 
Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Punjab and Rajasthan. 
India has been following a consistent policy for gradual removal of 
restrictions on imports since 1991. Tariff line-wise import policy was first 
announced on 31.3.1996. As on that date, import of 616 tariff lines (at 10 digit 
level) out of the total number of 10202 was free. Import restrictions on 488 
tariff lines were removed during the period 1.4.96 to 31.3.97. Further, 391 
tariff lines (at 8 digit level) were freed during the period 1.4.97 to 13.4.98 and 
894 tariff lines (at 8 digit level) were freed on 1.4.99. Thus removal of import 
restrictions on 714 tariff lines was nothing but a continuation of the stated 
policy of the Government. Import restrictions on the remaining 715 tariff lines are 
going to be removed on 31.3.2001. 
Import restrictions have been removed in line with the economic 
liberalisation policy being followed since 1991 and also in accordance with 
the country's commitments to the multilateral trading regime. Thus, the requests 
of the various State Governments regarding re-imposition of QRs could not be 
considered. However, in order to provide protection to the domestic producers the 
Government can, if the situation so warrants, utilise the mechanism of raising the 
applied tariffs within the bound rates, if such a gap exists and take measures such 
as anti-dumping action, imposition of counter-vailing duties and safeguard 
actions which are permissible under the WTO agreement. 
The imports are being closely monitored and the Government have been 
taking such steps, whenever warranted to ensure that imports do not cause and 
serious injury to the domestic producers.

NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANG WAR): (a) to (c) Nitish Sengupta

33.6% share holding of IBP to a strategic partner i.e. Bharat Petroleum 
Corporation Limited (BPCL) directly as permissible under the Securities 
Exchange Board of India (SEBI) take over guidelines. However, IBP Co. Limited

out of Government holding of 59% in IBP through strategic sale. The 
recommendation of Sengupta Committ ee and the report of Disinvestment 
Commission were examined by the Government and a final decision was taken 
to retain 26% of its equity in IBP and the balance to be disinvestcd to a strategic 
partner.
